cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: AURKA is a centrosome-associated serine/threonine kinase that governs centrosome maturation, mitotic spindle assembly, and cytokinesis, with additional non-mitotic roles in ciliary disassembly, spermatogenesis, and meiotic spindle organization [PMID:9771714, PMID:34518881, PMID:31895686]. It is activated at the centrosome and spindle by structurally distinct cofactors — TPX2, CEP192 (via a dedicated helix binding a site separate from TPX2), Ca²⁺/calmodulin, and Bora — and phosphorylates PLK1 to trigger mitotic entry, HDM2 to promote p53 ubiquitination, SPOP to stabilize AR and c-Myc, and KEAP1 to activate NRF2-dependent ferroptosis suppression [PMID:37083534, PMID:22621899, PMID:26779436, PMID:24240108, PMID:33158056, PMID:38642502]. AURKA protein levels are tightly controlled by degradative ubiquitination through APC/C-FZR1 and SMAD4-dependent proteasomal pathways, counterbalanced by stabilizing monoubiquitination from CBLC and deubiquitination by USP21 [PMID:30498084, PMID:25061104, PMID:35149839, PMID:36919585]. A non-mitotic nuclear pool of AURKA, promoted by TPX2 co-expression and impaired proteasomal clearance, partners with hnRNP K in a kinase-independent manner to transactivate MYC and with DDX5 to induce lncRNA transcription [PMID:26782714, PMID:36797043, PMID:37217070].

CDC27 (APC3) is a core TPR-repeat subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that drives mitotic progression by targeting cyclins, securin, and other substrates for proteasomal destruction. CDC27 homodimerizes through a conserved N-terminal TPR superhelix essential for function, and its C-terminal IR tail-binding cleft recruits the coactivators CDC20 and CDH1, while also mediating incorporation of APC16 and APC7 [PMID:7736580, PMID:20206185, PMID:25490258]. Cdk1 phosphorylation of CDC27 is required for its chromosomal localization during mitosis and for APC/C-dependent degradation of cyclin A and cyclin B, whereas casein kinase II phosphorylation at Ser154 activates APC/C toward the TGF-β effector SnoN; phosphatases PP5 and PP2A counteract these modifications [PMID:17519285, PMID:12953067, PMID:21209074, PMID:9405394]. CDC27 protein stability is maintained by O-GlcNAcylation that prevents autophagy-lysosome-mediated degradation, and its translation is post-transcriptionally repressed by HNRNP E1, whose loss causes constitutive APC/C activation, premature CDH1 destruction, and aneuploidy [PMID:39984622, PMID:27102006].

CENP-W is an inner kinetochore protein that heterodimerizes with CENP-T to form a stable complex essential for centromere-based chromosome segregation, bipolar spindle integrity, and kinetochore-microtubule attachment during mitosis [PMID:19533040, PMID:25329824, PMID:32446395]. Mutual stabilization of the CENP-T·CENP-W dimer protects both subunits from CSN5/JAB1-directed proteasomal degradation, and CENP-W protein stability during interphase further depends on nucleophosmin/B23, which anchors it in the nucleolus and nuclear matrix [PMID:23926101, PMID:22002061]. Beyond its structural kinetochore role, CENP-W negatively regulates SCFβ-TrCP1 ubiquitin ligase activity at the G2/M transition by competing with SKP1 for CUL1 binding, thereby stabilizing CDC25A and promoting mitotic entry [PMID:29863914]. CENP-W also associates with EZH2 at target gene promoters to enhance Polycomb-mediated transcriptional repression [PMID:26111449].

CEP192 is a centrosomal scaffold protein essential for pericentriolar material (PCM) assembly, centriole duplication, and mitotic spindle formation. It recruits γ-tubulin, pericentrin, and NEDD1 to build the PCM [PMID:17980596, PMID:18207742], and hierarchically positions Cep152 and Plk4 at centrioles via acidic N-terminal motifs to initiate centriole duplication [PMID:23641073, PMID:24277814]. CEP192 directly binds and activates Aurora A at centrosomes through a structurally distinct interface from TPX2, promoting Aurora A dimerization and activation-loop phosphorylation that primes the kinase pool subsequently transferred to spindle microtubules via TPX2 [PMID:21097701, PMID:37083534, PMID:39327527]. Its conserved SP2D domain adopts an extended-cradle fold whose PLK1-dependent phosphorylation drives higher-order oligomerization for PCM scaffold self-assembly, and CEP192 protein levels are regulated by PHD1/SCF(Skp2)- and FBXL13-mediated proteasomal degradation [PMID:40106572, PMID:23932902, PMID:29348145].

CKAP5 (ch-TOG/XMAP215) is a microtubule polymerase whose N-terminal TOG domains bind free tubulin with high affinity (~10 nM Kd) and catalyze microtubule elongation through an enzyme-like tubulin-shuttling mechanism at plus ends, with growth rate showing hyperbolic dependence on tubulin concentration [bio_10.1101_2025.06.09.658552]. Its C-terminal TOG5 domain binds the microtubule lattice to promote lateral tubulin–tubulin interactions, while its TOG6 domain anchors the protein to γ-TuRC via γ-tubulin, and both domains are required for cooperative microtubule nucleation from γ-TuRC [bio_10.1101_2024.06.03.597159]. The C-terminal α-helical bundle domain mediates the interaction with TACC3, and disruption of this interaction causes pericentriolar material fragmentation and delayed mitotic progression [bio_10.1101_2024.05.31.596836].

DLGAP5 (also known as HURP) is a mitotic microtubule-associated protein that stabilizes kinetochore fibers by preferentially binding the GDP-tubulin lattice, promotes branching microtubule nucleation synergistically with TPX2, and facilitates chromosome congression through interaction with Kif18A and TACC3 [PMID:35948594, PMID:39516491, PMID:21924616, PMID:30054275]. Its chromosome-proximal localization on spindle microtubules is established by the Ran-GTP/importin-β gradient, and Aurora A kinase phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain relieves autoinhibition of the N-terminal microtubule-binding domain, enabling spatially restricted microtubule stabilization [PMID:16631580, PMID:18321990, PMID:33186548]. DLGAP5 protein levels are controlled by Cdk1–cyclin B phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitination via the SCF(Fbx7) E3 ligase, and transcription is activated by c-Rel (NF-κB family) [PMID:15145941, PMID:21549688]. Hurp-knockout female mice are infertile owing to defective endometrial stromal proliferation required for uterine decidualization [PMID:18676373].

HAUS1 is a subunit of the eight-component human augmin complex that nucleates and amplifies spindle microtubules in cooperation with the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), thereby ensuring kinetochore fiber stability, bipolar spindle integrity, and faithful chromosome segregation [PMID:18443220, PMID:19369198]. The complex localizes to interphase centrosomes and mitotic spindle microtubules, and its disruption causes centrosome fragmentation, metaphase–anaphase delay, and cytokinesis failure — defects partly driven by unopposed NuMA activity [PMID:19427217, PMID:15082789]. Augmin's microtubule-binding activity is directly inhibited by importins and relieved by Ran-GTP, linking branching nucleation to the chromosomal Ran gradient [PMID:37357828]. Beyond mitosis, HAUS1-dependent γ-tubulin–mediated microtubule nucleation at presynaptic boutons controls synaptic vesicle transport and evoked exocytosis in hippocampal neurons [PMID:31813605].

HAUS2 is a core subunit of the eight-component human Augmin (HAUS) complex, which localizes to interphase centrosomes and mitotic spindle microtubules and recruits the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) to promote spindle microtubule nucleation [PMID:19369198, PMID:19427217]. Loss of the HAUS complex causes microtubule-dependent centrosome fragmentation, destabilization of kinetochore microtubules, multipolar spindle formation, spindle assembly checkpoint activation, and cytokinesis failure — defects that are rescued by co-depletion of NuMA, establishing that HAUS and NuMA exert opposing activities at the spindle [PMID:19427217, PMID:19369198]. In neural progenitor cells, HAUS2 depletion acts redundantly with HAUS5 loss, and combined knockdown causes centrosome fragmentation and cell lethality, underscoring context-dependent functional buffering among HAUS subunits [PMID:28596487].

HAUS3 is a constitutive subunit of the eight-subunit human augmin (HAUS) complex, which recruits the gamma-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) to spindle microtubules to drive centrosome-independent microtubule nucleation and amplification essential for mitotic spindle assembly, kinetochore fiber stability, chromosome segregation, and cytokinesis [PMID:18443220, PMID:19369198, PMID:19427217]. The complex localizes to interphase centrosomes and mitotic spindle microtubules; its disruption causes centrosome fragmentation, multipolar spindles, spindle checkpoint activation, and cytokinesis failure, with spindle-pole defects partially suppressed by co-depletion of NuMA [PMID:19427217, PMID:19369198]. Beyond mitosis, the HAUS complex organizes non-centrosomal microtubule arrays in post-mitotic neurons, where it is required for neuronal migration, axon development, dendritic branching, and uniform axonal microtubule polarity [PMID:30044976]. A zebrafish Haus3 loss-of-function mutant demonstrates a cell-autonomous requirement for HAUS3 in maintaining hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell pools during definitive hematopoiesis [PMID:21228005].

HAUS4 is a subunit of the eight-component human Augmin (HAUS) complex that promotes acentrosomal microtubule nucleation by recruiting the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) to existing spindle microtubules, thereby ensuring spindle integrity, proper kinetochore–microtubule attachment, and faithful cytokinesis [PMID:19369198, PMID:19427217]. HAUS4 localizes to interphase centrosomes and mitotic spindle microtubules, and its depletion—alone or in combination with other HAUS subunits—causes centrosome fragmentation, multipolar spindles, spindle checkpoint activation, and induction of cellular senescence via p16/p21 [PMID:19427217, PMID:32264951]. Beyond mitosis, the HAUS complex functions in post-mitotic neurons, where it colocalizes with γ-TuRC along neurites to drive non-centrosomal microtubule nucleation required for neuronal migration, axon polarization, and dendrite microtubule density [PMID:30044976].

cluster_genes.UniProt_functional_annotation: Contributes to mitotic spindle assembly, maintenance of centrosome integrity and completion of cytokinesis as part of the HAUS augmin-like complex

cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: HAUS6 is a core subunit of the eight-membered augmin (HAUS) complex that drives microtubule-dependent microtubule nucleation on the mitotic spindle, amplifying spindle microtubule mass, sustaining kinetochore fiber formation, and enabling bipolar spindle assembly and cytokinesis [PMID:18443220, PMID:19369198, PMID:19427217]. Its conserved calponin homology (CH) domain directly contacts the microtubule lattice to anchor the complex and establish the shallow branch angle of newly nucleated microtubules, while specific regions of HAUS6 form a direct interface with γ-TuRC components to recruit the nucleation machinery to spindle microtubules [PMID:28351835, PMID:41173848]. Augmin activity is spatiotemporally regulated by Aurora-A phosphorylation of the Hice1 subunit, by Plk1-mediated recruitment, and by the inner nuclear membrane protein Samp1 [PMID:21705324, PMID:19596795, PMID:29514856]. Conditional loss of Haus6 in mouse neural progenitors triggers p53-dependent apoptosis and aborts brain development, and HAUS6 mutations have been identified in infertile patients with oocyte/embryo defects [PMID:34427181, PMID:39172836].

HAUS7 is a subunit of the augmin complex that promotes γ-tubulin-dependent microtubule nucleation in both dividing and post-mitotic cells. During meiosis, HAUS7 localizes to the spindle and is required for proper spindle formation, chromosome alignment, and γ-tubulin organization at spindle poles [PMID:23182369]. In neurons, HAUS7-dependent augmin activity drives de novo nucleation of distally oriented dynamic microtubules at presynaptic boutons, thereby controlling bidirectional synaptic vesicle transport and evoked exocytosis [PMID:31813605]. HAUS7 directly binds DOCK3, which transports it to neuronal growth cones; TrkB-mediated phosphorylation of DOCK3 at Y562 triggers HAUS7 dissociation, enabling local microtubule assembly required for axon regeneration after optic nerve injury [PMID:40712007].

HAUS8 (Hice1) is a subunit of the eight-membered augmin complex that enables microtubule-dependent microtubule nucleation within the mitotic spindle, thereby sustaining spindle architecture, poleward flux, and faithful chromosome segregation. Its disordered N-terminus constitutes a direct microtubule-binding site—structurally resolved by cryo-EM—that bundles and stabilizes microtubules and contributes to the shallow branch angle of newly nucleated microtubules, while its coiled-coil domain interacts with Hec1 to support centrosomal microtubule nucleation [PMID:18362163, PMID:19776357, PMID:41173848]. HAUS8 microtubule-binding activity is spatiotemporally regulated: Aurora-A phosphorylation of the N-terminal Ser/Thr cluster reduces microtubule affinity near spindle poles, Plk1 phosphorylation promotes augmin–microtubule interaction for intraspindle nucleation, and importin-α/β binding to two NLS sequences overlapping the microtubule-binding site globally inhibits augmin until local Ran-GTP release around chromosomes licenses branched nucleation [PMID:21705324, PMID:21690413, PMID:37086784, PMID:37357828]. HAUS8 also associates with the VISA/MAVS antiviral signaling complex and positively regulates virus-induced IFN-β induction [PMID:29916539].

KIF11 (Eg5) is a plus-end-directed kinesin-5 motor essential for centrosome separation, bipolar mitotic spindle assembly, and spindle elongation during cell division. Its spindle recruitment is controlled by CDK1 phosphorylation at Thr926/927 and Nek6/7 phosphorylation at Ser1033 downstream of a Plk1–Nek9 cascade, while PP2A/B55α dephosphorylates Thr926 to promote mitotic exit; additional post-translational regulation includes HDAC1-mediated deacetylation that modulates ATPase activity and RNF20/40-dependent monoubiquitination that stabilizes the protein [PMID:7753799, PMID:21642957, PMID:21522128, PMID:28487562, PMID:28392145, PMID:27557628]. KIF11 sliding forces are functionally balanced by the minus-end motor HSET, opposed by Tiam1–Rac1 signaling, dampened by HMMR-mediated TPX2 inhibitory complexes, and supplemented by a parallel Kif15–TPX2 sliding module and a PRC1–KIF4A module during anaphase [PMID:10525540, PMID:20346677, PMID:29386294, PMID:19818618, PMID:33910056]. Beyond mitosis, KIF11 transports β-actin mRNA in a ZBP1-dependent manner to regulate cell polarity and migration, promotes dendrite morphogenesis via NEK7 phosphorylation-dependent microtubule regulation, and acts as an inhibitory constraint on excitatory synaptic transmission in hippocampal neurons [PMID:25588836, PMID:29899413, PMID:30479371].

KIF18A is a plus-end-directed kinesin-8 family motor that accumulates along kinetochore microtubule (K-MT) bundles in a gradient and suppresses microtubule plus-end dynamics, thereby dampening chromosome oscillations and promoting chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate [PMID:17346968, PMID:18267093, PMID:22595673]. Its processivity and plus-end accumulation depend on a C-terminal non-motor microtubule-binding domain and an extended neck linker that enables navigation past microtubule-associated proteins, while the N-terminal motor domain directly caps and pauses growing plus ends in a concentration-dependent manner [PMID:21884977, PMID:20153196, PMID:30655363]. KIF18A activity is temporally regulated by antagonistic Cdk1 phosphorylation (inhibitory) and PP1γ dephosphorylation (activating), and is further modulated by the microtubule-associated protein HURP, which activates KIF18A at low density but sterically blocks it at high density [PMID:25048371, PMID:39516196]. Inhibition of KIF18A ATPase activity—at the α-4 helix/tubulin interface resolved by crystallography—selectively kills chromosomally unstable cancer cells by triggering widespread spindle-assembly checkpoint activation and lethal mitotic arrest [PMID:33619254, PMID:38151625, PMID:41257005].

NDC1 is a conserved multi-pass transmembrane nucleoporin that anchors nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) in the nuclear envelope by bridging the lipid bilayer to soluble scaffold nucleoporins. Its six N-terminal transmembrane segments embed it in the nuclear envelope membrane, where it directly binds Nup53 — an interaction essential for vertebrate NPC assembly that modulates Nup53's membrane-deforming activity — and forms additional complexes with transmembrane pore proteins Pom152/Pom34 and soluble Nup53/Nup59-Nup170 modules in yeast [PMID:16600873, PMID:19414609, PMID:24363447]. NDC1 determines NPC density independently of membrane biogenesis and recruits ALADIN to pores; in yeast it additionally mediates spindle pole body insertion into the nuclear envelope, with its partitioning between SPBs and NPCs controlled by interaction with the SUN-domain protein Mps3 [PMID:8349727, PMID:35852146, PMID:19782045, PMID:24515347]. Biallelic NDC1 variants that disrupt ALADIN binding cause decreased NPC insertion and ALADIN mislocalization in patient fibroblasts, establishing NDC1 as the causal gene for a triple A-like neuropathy syndrome [PMID:39003500].

NDC80 (Hec1) is the core microtubule-binding subunit of the conserved heterotetrameric NDC80 complex (Hec1–Nuf2–Spc24–Spc25), which forms the primary load-bearing link between kinetochores and spindle microtubules during chromosome segregation. The complex is an elongated rod (~570 Å) in which the Spc24–Spc25 end anchors to centromeric chromatin via CENP-T/Cnn1 and the Mis12/MIND complex, while the Hec1–Nuf2 end contacts microtubules through tandem calponin-homology (CH) domains and a positively charged, disordered N-terminal tail whose affinity is tuned by graded Aurora B and Aurora A phosphorylation to enable error correction of improper attachments [PMID:18455984, PMID:17129782, PMID:29187526, PMID:25808492]. Multivalent arrays of NDC80 complexes, organized through CENP-T– and Mis12-dependent recruitment of multiple copies per binding site, together with loop-mediated Ndc80–Ndc80 cooperativity and accessory factors (Dam1/DASH ring in yeast, Ska complex in metazoans), generate force-resistant end-on attachments that couple microtubule depolymerization to chromosome movement [PMID:29629870, PMID:37203876, PMID:38060647, PMID:28535377]. The NDC80 complex additionally scaffolds spindle checkpoint signaling by recruiting Mad1/Mad2 and Mps1 to unattached kinetochores, linking attachment status to mitotic checkpoint control [PMID:12351790, PMID:12514103].

NEDD1 (GCP-WD) is a WD40-repeat adaptor protein that targets the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) to centrosomes, spindle microtubules, and acentrosomal nucleation sites, thereby governing microtubule nucleation in both mitosis and meiosis [PMID:16378099, PMID:16461362]. Its C-terminal helical domain forms a tetramer that docks into the lumen of the γ-TuRC cone via MZT1–GCP3 modules anchored to GCP4/5/6, while its N-terminal WD40 β-propeller binds microtubules and the Augmin complex to support branched microtubule nucleation [PMID:39574704, PMID:41387433, PMID:36318115]. NEDD1 function is regulated by sequential mitotic phosphorylation: Plk1→Nek9 phosphorylates S377 for centrosomal γ-TuRC recruitment, Aurora A phosphorylates S405 for chromosome-proximal and midzone microtubule nucleation, S411 phosphorylation drives microtubule branching, and PLK4 phosphorylates S325 to promote SAS-6 recruitment and centriole duplication [PMID:22818914, PMID:23273898, PMID:36318115, PMID:33351100]. MZT1 stabilizes NEDD1 protein by inhibiting its ubiquitination, and loss of NEDD1 causes monopolar spindles, aneuploidy, and premature senescence [PMID:40204068, PMID:20079731, PMID:21364642].

NUF2 is a core structural subunit of the NDC80 kinetochore complex that is essential for chromosome segregation during cell division and also contributes to interphase ribosome biogenesis. NUF2 heterodimerizes with NDC80/Hec1 through a coiled-coil interface stabilized by buried Glu-Lys pairs, and this dimer forms the outer plate of the kinetochore where it directly engages spindle microtubule walls via the calponin-homology (CH) domains of both subunits; the Nuf2 CH domain specifically generates interkinetochore tension and acts as a force-dependent friction regulator enabling bidirectional kinetochore sliding along microtubules [PMID:24129578, PMID:21270439, PMID:15548592]. NUF2 recruits CENP-E to kinetochores through mitosis-specific poly-SUMO-2/3 modification that engages CENP-E's SUMO-interacting motif, retains spindle checkpoint proteins Mad1/Mad2 against microtubule-dependent stripping, and during interphase supports pre-rRNA transcription by maintaining RNA Pol I largest subunit levels [PMID:33910471, PMID:14654001, PMID:39705402]. A de novo missense variant disrupting the NUF2 CH domain causes destabilization of the NDC80–NUF2 heterodimer, aneuploidy, and a human syndrome of microcephaly and short stature, establishing NUF2 as the first NDC80 complex member linked to a Mendelian disorder [PMID:33721060].

PLK1 is a master mitotic serine/threonine kinase that orchestrates centrosome maturation, spindle assembly, kinetochore–microtubule attachment, chromosome integrity, cytokinesis, and centromeric CENP-A deposition through phosphorylation of a broad substrate repertoire. PLK1 activation requires Aurora-A–mediated phosphorylation of T210 in a process primed by CDK1-phosphorylated Bora/SPAT-1, and this activation operates as a bistable switch controlled by a dimerization-to-monomer transition that gates nuclear entry [PMID:25753036, PMID:34759346, PMID:24338364]. At kinetochores, PLK1 is recruited via its polo-box domain (PBD) to CDK1/self-primed phosphodocking sites on BUB1, CENP-U, CLIP-170, and PBIP1, and is removed by non-proteolytic CUL3–KLHL22 ubiquitylation at K492; its kinase output is further tuned by SETD6 methylation (K209/K413), SET7/9 dimethylation (K191), PTEN-dependent dephosphorylation, and an Apolo1–PP1γ feedback loop [PMID:33248027, PMID:23455478, PMID:30622182, PMID:31863092, PMID:34260926]. Beyond mitotic progression, PLK1 phosphorylates p53 and TAp63 to suppress apoptosis, phosphorylates Mre11 to terminate DNA-damage checkpoints, activates Polθ for mitotic DNA repair, restricts PrimPol chromatin loading to prevent replication-associated breaks, promotes CENP-A deposition by activating the Mis18 complex, and coordinates nuclear pore complex disassembly at mitotic entry [PMID:15024021, PMID:19668228, PMID:28512243, PMID:37674080, PMID:34860556, PMID:39236163, PMID:29487689].

SASS6 (SAS-6) is the master structural scaffold of the centriolar cartwheel, whose self-assembly into 9-fold symmetric ring polymers establishes the fundamental radial symmetry of centrioles and is essential for centriole biogenesis across eukaryotes. The N-terminal globular domain mediates head-to-head dimerization that drives ring formation, while the coiled-coil domain enables asymmetric homo-oligomerization that imparts polarity and supports ring stacking into the cartwheel hub; point mutations at either interface abolish centriole assembly in vivo [PMID:21273447, PMID:35240058, PMID:26002084]. SAS-6 is recruited to the mother centriole through direct binding of the ZYG-1/PLK4 kinase and PLK4-phosphorylated SAS-5/Ana2/STIL to its coiled-coil region, and its C-terminal tail anchors the γ-tubulin ring complex to nucleate centriolar microtubules [PMID:23673331, PMID:25264260, PMID:32442461]. SAS-6 protein levels are tightly controlled by APC/C-Cdh1 degradation in late mitosis/G1 and FBXW7-mediated ubiquitination of the STIL–SAS-6 complex to prevent centriole overduplication, while CDK-1 phosphorylation of its C-terminus inhibits phase separation to promote timely centriole disassembly during oogenesis [PMID:40825584, PMID:41453690, PMID:40410380].

SKA1 is the microtubule-binding subunit of the heterotrimeric Ska complex (Ska1–Ska2–Ska3) that functions at the kinetochore–microtubule interface to enable faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The Ska1 microtubule-binding domain engages both straight microtubule lattice and curved protofilaments at depolymerizing ends, enabling processive tracking of dynamic plus-ends; this activity is enhanced by cooperative oligomerization with the Ndc80 complex, which stabilizes lateral tubulin protofilament contacts at microtubule tips, and by formation of a tripartite Ndc80–Cdt1–Ska1 complex [PMID:19289083, PMID:23085020, PMID:37265445]. Ska3 allosterically modulates Ska1's tubulin-binding surfaces, EB1 recruits the Ska complex to kinetochores through a conserved N-terminal motif on Ska1, and Aurora B phosphorylation regulates the microtubule-binding domain, collectively ensuring proper kinetochore–microtubule attachment and timely spindle-checkpoint silencing [PMID:27667719, PMID:36592928, PMID:17093495]. Ska1 overexpression drives centrosome amplification via centriole over-duplication, linking its dysregulation to chromosomal instability and tumorigenesis [PMID:24827423].

SKA2 is a multifunctional protein that participates in mitotic checkpoint silencing as a subunit of the SKA1/SKA2 spindle–kinetochore complex and acts as a glucocorticoid receptor (GR) co-activator in postmitotic cells by promoting GR–FKBP4 interaction and displacing FKBP5, thereby tuning HPA axis negative feedback [PMID:17093495, PMID:18583474, PMID:39705315]. In microglia, SKA2 suppresses FKBP5-dependent secretory autophagy and NLRP3/Gasdermin D–mediated IL-1β release, and its loss drives neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration [PMID:38528004]. SKA2 also functions outside the spindle context as a transcriptional co-regulator that associates with Sp1 to repress PDSS2 and upregulates SLC6A9 to sustain glutathione-dependent redox homeostasis [PMID:36860919, PMID:41847110]. Transcription of the PRR11–SKA2 bidirectional locus is directly controlled by NF-Y, indirectly repressed by p53 via NF-Y displacement, and co-regulated by HIF-1α/PPAR-α and intronic miRNA circuits [PMID:26162986, PMID:28257042, PMID:26460070].

SKA3 is a core subunit of the trimeric Ska complex (Ska1–Ska2–Ska3) that stabilizes kinetochore–microtubule attachments and promotes spindle assembly checkpoint silencing during mitosis. SKA3 directly contacts tubulin and allosterically modulates Ska1 microtubule-binding activity; Cdk1-dependent phosphorylation of SKA3 enables direct binding to the Ndc80 complex, recruiting the Ska complex to kinetochores, while Aurora B phosphorylation opposes this recruitment [PMID:19360002, PMID:27667719, PMID:28479321]. Depletion of SKA3 destabilizes kinetochore fibres, activates the spindle checkpoint, and arrests cells in metaphase [PMID:19646878, PMID:19387489]. Outside mitosis, SKA3 stabilizes PLK1 by suppressing its ubiquitin-mediated degradation and, under hypoxia, scaffolds PARP1–HIF-1α complexes to promote HIF-1α stabilization and glycolytic or lipogenic gene expression in cancer cells [PMID:33106477, PMID:37821935, PMID:41298345].

SPC24 is a conserved subunit of the NDC80 kinetochore complex that is essential for accurate chromosome segregation during cell division. SPC24 physically interacts with NDC80, NUF2, and SPC25 to form the heterotetrameric NDC80 complex, localizes to kinetochores, and is required for stable kinetochore–microtubule attachment, recruitment of the spindle assembly checkpoint protein Mad2, and kinetochore localization of the microtubule-associated factor Stu2/XMAP215 [PMID:11952896, PMID:27713128, PMID:17507656]. Loss of SPC24 causes premature spindle expansion during S-phase arrest, chromosome misalignment, accelerated meiosis I, and high rates of aneuploidy [PMID:17507656, PMID:27713128]. SPC24 expression is transcriptionally regulated by E2F7 and the lncRNA LINC02154, and post-transcriptionally controlled by miR-7-5p targeting and METTL14-mediated m6A-dependent mRNA degradation [PMID:35543858, PMID:34020142, PMID:40663204, PMID:40848939].

SPC25 is a core subunit of the NDC80 kinetochore complex that functions in chromosome alignment, spindle assembly, and spindle checkpoint signaling during cell division, and additionally serves as a scaffolding platform for oncogenic signaling complexes in multiple cancer contexts. At the kinetochore, SPC25 partners with NDC80, NUF2, and SPC24 to ensure faithful chromosome segregation; its perturbation in mouse oocytes causes spindle disruption and chromosome misalignment [PMID:21084868], and the SPC25/NUF2 interaction drives cancer cell proliferation and glycolysis [PMID:39755832]. Beyond mitosis, SPC25 assembles a trimeric SPC25/RIOK1/MYH9 complex that activates Wnt/β-catenin signaling through RIOK1-mediated phosphorylation of MYH9, promoting cancer stemness and platinum resistance [PMID:39488790], and it stabilizes E2F1 by blocking MDM2-mediated ubiquitination, thereby upregulating CCND1 [PMID:39919356]. SPC25 expression is transcriptionally activated by E2F8 and TFDP1, linking its regulation to cell-cycle transcription factor networks, and its downstream effects include activation of FAK/PI3K/AKT and DNA-PK/AKT/Notch1 cascades, promotion of glycolysis, suppression of ferroptosis, and modulation of anti-tumor immunity through glutamine metabolism [PMID:39829079, PMID:36147467, PMID:39558547].

SPDL1 (Spindly) is a coiled-coil kinetochore adaptor essential for recruiting the dynein/dynactin motor complex to kinetochores downstream of the RZZ (Rod–Zwilch–Zw10) complex, thereby coupling chromosome movement to spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) silencing during mitosis [PMID:18765790, PMID:19468067]. A conserved Spindly motif is required for dynein recruitment but not for kinetochore localization; upon microtubule attachment, dynein strips Spindly together with MAD1–MAD2 and RZZ from bioriented kinetochores, and this removal—not poleward transport per se—is the critical event that terminates checkpoint signaling [PMID:20439434, PMID:20427577]. Beyond mitosis, SPDL1 suppresses invasion and migration in colorectal cancer cells by restraining EGFR/ERK signaling downstream of MRTFB [PMID:31690663, PMID:40487946], and a distinct isoform (SPDL1-L) localizes to lipid droplets in cone photoreceptors where it recruits centrins to control droplet positioning and light sensitivity [PMID:37699389].

STIL is a core centriole duplication factor that orchestrates procentriole biogenesis by serving as a central scaffold linking PLK4 kinase activation, cartwheel assembly, and centriole wall formation, while its levels are tightly controlled across the cell cycle to ensure numerically precise centriole duplication. STIL directly binds and activates PLK4, which in turn phosphorylates STIL at the STAN motif to enable SAS6 recruitment for cartwheel assembly and at S428 to promote CPAP binding for linking the cartwheel to centriolar microtubules [PMID:26101219, PMID:31115335]. STIL exerts bimodal control over PLK4—its coiled-coil domain stabilizes PLK4 at the procentriole site while its TIM domain promotes degradation of adjacent PLK4—thereby restricting formation to a single daughter centriole per parent [PMID:29898389]. STIL protein abundance is regulated by APC/C-Cdh1-dependent degradation via a C-terminal KEN box at mitotic exit, SCF-βTrCP-dependent degradation via a DSG motif during interphase (antagonized by CDK2), and USP9X-mediated deubiquitylation at centrosomes; additionally, STIL is essential for primary cilia formation and Sonic Hedgehog signaling downstream of Patched, connecting centriole biology to developmental patterning [PMID:24485834, PMID:29445034, PMID:31197030, PMID:10385121, PMID:25486474].

TACC3 is a centrosomal and mitotic spindle adaptor protein that orchestrates microtubule organization, kinetochore fiber stability, and translational control during cell division. Aurora A kinase phosphorylates TACC3 at Ser558 (human), inducing a conformational switch that enables binding to clathrin heavy chain; the resulting TACC3–ch-TOG–clathrin complex forms inter-microtubule bridges within kinetochore fibers essential for spindle integrity and metaphase tension [PMID:20566684, PMID:21297582, PMID:29510984]. Independent of clathrin, a TACC3–ch-TOG pool tracks microtubule plus ends to promote polymerization, while TACC3 also facilitates γ-tubulin ring complex assembly for centrosomal microtubule nucleation [PMID:25187649, PMID:25246530]. Beyond mitosis, TACC3 regulates CPE-dependent mRNA translation (notably cyclin B1) through its Xenopus ortholog maskin's eIF4E-sequestering activity, and in interphase it interacts with the NuRD complex to repress tumor suppressor transcription and with Notch intracellular domains to negatively regulate Notch signaling [PMID:12110596, PMID:36864125, PMID:20804727].

TUBGCP4 (GCP4) is a core structural subunit of the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) that is essential for microtubule nucleation, spindle assembly, and γ-TuRC integrity. Its C-terminal grip2 domain directly binds γ-tubulin, as defined by crystal structure, and it forms a salt-resistant sub-complex with GCP5 and GCP6 (stoichiometry 2:1:1) that scaffolds γ-TuRC assembly from γ-tubulin small complexes (γTuSCs) [PMID:21725292, PMID:32317396]. Beyond microtubule nucleation, GCP4 inhibits autophagy by competing with ATG3 for binding to ATG7, thereby blocking LC3B lipidation; complete knockout in mice is embryonic lethal due to spindle defects, while haploinsufficiency causes photoreceptor degeneration through dysregulated autophagy [PMID:31209365]. Loss-of-function mutations in TUBGCP4 cause autosomal recessive microcephaly with reduced γ-TuRC levels, impaired microtubule nucleation, and aneuploidy in patient fibroblasts [PMID:25817018].

TUBGCP6 is the largest subunit of the γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), serving as a structural scaffold essential for γ-TuRC assembly, microtubule nucleation, centriole duplication, and spindle integrity. GCP6 carries a unique extended insertion domain that stabilizes a GCP2-3-4-5-4-6 core around which four GCP2-GCP3 units are recruited stepwise to complete the 14-spoked asymmetric spiral of the γ-TuRC, and it forms a salt-resistant sub-complex with GCP4 and GCP5 that is independently assembled prior to full γ-TuRC formation [PMID:31856152, PMID:32317396, PMID:35078983]. GCP6 is phosphorylated by PLK4 to regulate centriole duplication, binds keratins via its C-terminus to anchor MTOCs apically in polarized epithelial cells (a function released by Cdk1 phosphorylation at S1397), and its protein levels are controlled post-transcriptionally through splicing of its pre-mRNA by WBP11 and SF3B14 [PMID:22302995, PMID:17182859, PMID:31874114]. Biallelic mutations in TUBGCP6 cause microcephalic primordial dwarfism with retinopathy, establishing it as a disease gene in the PLK4–centriole duplication pathway [PMID:25344692].
